    AI Overview
    Rotavirus is a highly contagious virus causing severe, watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain, primarily in infants and young children. Transmitted via the fecal-oral route or contaminated surfaces, it frequently leads to severe dehydration and hospitalization. Treatment focuses on hydration, as no specific medicine exists, but vaccines are effective for prevention. 
    Key Details About Rotavirus 
    • Symptoms: Intense, watery diarrhea (often 6+ times in 24 hours), vomiting, high fever (
      ), stomach pain, and dehydration. Symptoms usually appear 1-2 days after exposure and last 3-8 days.
    • Transmission: Highly contagious, spreading via the fecal-oral route—often when contaminated hands, objects (toys), or food touch the mouth. It can survive on surfaces for weeks.
    • Complications: Severe dehydration, which can be fatal, is the main complication. It causes 20-40 deaths and 50,000+ hospitalizations in the US annually.
    • Diagnosis: Doctors typically diagnose it based on symptoms, but it can be confirmed via a stool test.
    • Treatment: There is no specific medication to treat the virus. Management focuses on preventing dehydration by increasing fluid intake or using IV fluids.
    • Prevention: Vaccination is the most effective method, with two safe and effective vaccines (RotaTeq and Rotarix) approved for infants. Frequent handwashing is crucial. 
    Rotavirus is most common from January to June. While it affects all ages, it is most severe in children, particularly those unvaccinated.

    AI Overview
    Rotavirus symptoms include sudden onset of severe, watery diarrhea (lasting 3–8 days), vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain. It causes acute gastroenteritis, often leading to rapid dehydration, especially in infants. Symptoms typically appear 1–3 days after exposure, often beginning with vomiting. 
    Key Symptoms of Rotavirus: 
    • Watery Diarrhea: Frequently severe and lasting 3 to 8 days.
    • Vomiting: Often the first symptom to appear.
    • Fever: Usually subsides within the first couple of days.
    • Abdominal Pain/Cramping: Common along with the infection.
    • Loss of Appetite: Common, particularly in children.
    Signs of Dehydration (Major Complication):
    Rotavirus can cause severe fluid loss, requiring close monitoring: 
    • Infants: Few or no tears when crying, dry mouth/throat, reduced urination (fewer than 4-6 wet diapers in 24 hours), or sunken eyes/soft spot. 
    • Children/Adults: Lethargy, dizziness, unusual sleepiness, or fussiness. 
    Usage Examples/Context:
    • Infection Timeframe:
      Symptoms usually start two days after exposure, with diarrhea lasting 3–8 days. 
    • Affected Population:
      Nearly all children are infected before age 5, with high vulnerability in infants under 6 months. 
    Synonyms/Related Terms: Acute gastroenteritis, Stomach bug / Stomach flu, Infantile diarrhea, and Rotaviral enteritis. 
    Disclaimer: Seek immediate medical attention if a child has a fever over
    102∘F102 raised to the composed with power cap F
    (
    38.9∘C38.9 raised to the composed with power cap C
    )    , blood/pus in stool, or signs of severe dehydration.

      Vaccine. What is the rotavirus vaccine?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      The rotavirus vaccine is an oral, live-attenuated vaccine given to infants to prevent severe diarrhea, vomiting, and dehydration caused by rotavirus. It is highly effective, protecting about 98% of babies from severe disease. The vaccine is given as drops in the mouth, not as a shot, usually in 2 or 3 doses starting at 2 months of age. 
      Key Details About Rotavirus Vaccines:
      • Vaccine Types:
        There are two main types used in the US: RotaTeq (RV5) (three doses at 2, 4, and 6 months) and Rotarix (RV1) (two doses at 2 and 4 months). 
      • Target Group:
        Infants, with the first dose typically administered between 6 and 15 weeks of age, and the full series completed by 8 months. 
      • Effectiveness:
        It is highly effective, with
        85%–95%85 % – 95 %
        reduction in severe diarrhea and hospitalizations in many countries.         
      • Safety:
        It is considered safe and effective, with a very rare risk of a stomach condition called intussusception (approx. 1–6 per 100,000 infants). 
      • Why It's Given:
        Before vaccines, rotavirus caused widespread severe diarrhea and hospitalization in children worldwide. 
      The vaccine works by stimulating the immune system to create antibodies against the virus without causing a full infection.

        Complications. What are the complications of rotavirus?
        About this result
        Feedback
        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        Rotavirus complications mainly stem from severe gastroenteritis, causing dangerous dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and metabolic acidosis, particularly in infants. Common severe complications include hospitalization due to intense vomiting/diarrhea, and rarely, seizure-related neurological issues, intestinal blockage (intussusception), or death. 
        Key Complications of Rotavirus:
        • Severe Dehydration:
          The most common complication, indicated by dry mouth, low urine output, sunken eyes, and lack of tears. 
        • Electrolyte Imbalance:
          Loss of potassium, sodium, and chloride through diarrhea can affect heart and brain function. 
        • Neurological Complications:
          These can include benign seizures (convulsions), meningitis, encephalitis (brain swelling), or encephalopathy, particularly in children. 
        • Intestinal Blockage (Intussusception):
          A rare but serious condition where part of the intestine telescopes into another, requiring immediate medical care. 
        • Metabolic Acidosis:
          An increase in acid levels in the body due to severe diarrhea and dehydration. 
        • Temporary Lactose Intolerance:
          The virus can destroy enzymes that break down dairy products, causing temporary intolerance. 
        • Persistent Disease:
          Immunocompromised individuals may experience prolonged or systemic rotavirus infections that affect multiple organ systems. 
        Note: Rotavirus vaccines are highly effective at preventing severe cases and these complications, say CDC reports.

          Risk Factors. What are the risk factors for rotavirus?
          About this result

          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          Rotavirus is highly contagious, primarily affecting unvaccinated infants and young children aged 3 months to 3 years, particularly in daycare settings. Key risk factors include lack of breastfeeding, poor sanitation, and close contact with infected individuals. It spreads via the fecal-oral route, with outbreaks common in winter. 
          Key Risk Factors for Rotavirus Infection:
          • Age and Vaccination Status: Unvaccinated infants and children (3 months to 3 years) are most vulnerable. 
          • Daycare/Childcare Attendance: High population density in daycares allows rapid spread. 
          • Lack of Breastfeeding: Infants not exclusively breastfed, especially in the first 6 months, face higher risks. 
          • Poor Hygiene and Sanitation: Lack of handwashing after diaper changes or before feeding. 
          • Environmental Exposure: Contaminated surfaces, food, or water. 
          • Weakened Immune System: Immunocompromised children or adults are more susceptible. 
          Synonyms/Related Risk Factors: Infantile gastroenteritis risk factors, Fecal-oral transmission hazards, Immunocompromised susceptibility, and Unvaccinated status.
          Usage Examples of Risk Factors:
          • Scenario 1: A 10-month-old child in a crowded daycare center contracts the virus. 
          • Scenario 2: An infant who is formula-fed instead of breastfed is exposed to the virus. 
          • Scenario 3: A child in a household where a sibling has diarrhea, and handwashing is not frequent. 
          • Scenario 4: An unvaccinated child during winter months, when rotavirus activity peaks. 
          Disclaimer: Rotavirus infections can lead to severe diarrhea and dehydration. Prompt medical attention is necessary if symptoms are severe.

            Feedback

            People also ask
            How common is rotavirus?
            Rotavirus causes more than 125 million cases of diarrhea each year in children and infants worldwide. In the United States, the number of childhood deaths from rotavirus is between 20 to 40 each year (compared to 600,000 worldwide).

            Rotavirus Infections | Boston Children's Hospital


            Boston Children's Hospital
            https://www.childrenshospital.org › conditions-treatments
            Boston Children's Hospital
            https://www.childrenshospital.org › conditions-treatments
            How long does rotavirus last in adults?
            Rotavirus is a virus that causes diarrheal illness. It is most common in infants and young children, and can be severe in these populations. Older children and adults can also become infected, but illness is usually not as severe as in younger children. Symptoms usually last three to eight days.

            How does a person get rotavirus?
            You can get rotavirus if you get virus particles in your mouth by: Putting your unwashed hands that are contaminated with poop into your mouth. Touching contaminated objects or surfaces and then putting your fingers in your mouth. Eating contaminated food.Apr 22, 2024

            Can you have rotavirus without vomiting?
            In adults, rotavirus infection doesn't tend to causes symptoms or causes mild symptoms. In children and others, symptoms often start within two days of exposure to the virus. Symptoms include: Fever and vomiting.Aug 18, 2025
